paper_title: RynnWorld-Latent: A Cross-Embodiment World Model Conditioned on Universal Latent Actions

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: World models, which predict future states conditioned on actions, have long been theorized as cornerstone of generalist robot intelligence (Sutton, 1991; LeCun et al., 2022; Richens et al., 2025). The recent progress of large-scale video generation has catalyzed new class of video world models, in which future dynamics are represented directly in visual space (Zhao et al., 2026b,c; Agarwal et al., 2025; Ali et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026e,a, 2025). These models achieve impressive visual fidelity and provide promising substrate for learning physical dynamics from large-scale video corpora. However, when applied to robotic manipulation, language-conditioned video generators face an interface mismatch: their primary control signal is task-level description, while physical interaction is governed by continuous, frame-level causal interventions. Language describes semantic intentions at coarse temporal granularity. An instruction such as pick up the cup specifies task outcome, but does not determine the precise trajectory by which the outcome is achieved. In contact-rich manipulation, small differences in timing, contact order, gripper state, or camera motion can lead to substantially different futures. Without fine-grained motion or action conditioning, text-conditioned model must represent multiple plausible trajectories for the same instruction, making precise control over manipulation dynamics challenging. Moreover, natural language alone is not convenient interface for specifying temporally precise interventions, such as closing the gripper earlier while maintaining the same preceding motion. These limitations motivate an explicit action-conditioning interface for controllable video world modeling. natural solution is to condition world models on robot actions (Gao et al., 2026). However, directly using raw robot actions introduces severe alignment bottleneck. Different embodiments operate in heterogeneous kinematic spaces, with different joint counts, coordinate conventions, control frequencies, and hardware limits. As result, world model conditioned on raw actions is difficult to scale across platforms. At the same time, large-scale human videos contain abundant interaction dynamics without robot-specific control labels, while simulation actions need not match target robots control space. What is needed is not stronger action encoder for particular robot, but shared action interface that represents interaction-related visual change while abstracting away platform-specific control conventions. We argue that latent actions provide such an interface. Instead of representing actions as robot commands, latent actions describe what changed between observations. Distilled from video in self-supervised manner, continuous latent actions provide shared description of visual transitions without requiring identical hardware control interfaces. Human hands, robot grippers, and simulated agents may differ drastically in their lowlevel control signals, yet their visual transitions can share motion and interaction patterns. By encoding heterogeneous videos into shared latent-action representation, single world model can be pretrained on human interactions, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts under unified action-conditioning objective, without requiring their native control spaces to be aligned. In this work, we introduce RynnWorld-Latent, cross-embodiment video world model built upon RynnLAM (Zhao et al., 2026d), the 3D-grounded latent-action representation introduced in RynnVLA-Latent (Zhao et al., 2026d). While RynnVLA-Latent (Zhao et al., 2026d) uses these descriptors as supervision targets for policy pretraining, our work investigates their complementary role as conditioning signals for learning controllable visual dynamics. RynnWorld-Latent predicts future video from an initial observation and sequence of continuous latent actions, without requiring text conditioning or common native robot action space. Technically, we combine global action tokens with an identity-initialized, frame-aligned local conditioning pathway within pretrained video diffusion transformer. The local pathway exploits the temporal correspondence between latent-action extraction and video-latent compression, allowing each action descriptor to condition its corresponding future video latent. central idea of this work is that RynnWorld-Latent should not be viewed only as future predictor, but as data-generation engine for scalable robot learning. This leads to two complementary generation modes. First, after target-robot post-training, RynnWorld-Latent can be conditioned on target robot actions and support interactive digital teleoperation (Zhao et al., 2026c): operator control signals are mapped to target actions and drive video generation, producing paired action-video data without requiring additional physical robot execution. Second, the latent-action-conditioned model enables data synthesis from existing videos. Given source video, we extract its latent-action sequence, edit the first frame to replace the embodiment or environment, and generate new rollout conditioned on the edited first frame and the original latent actions. First-frame editing specifies the new visual embodiment or environment, while the latent-action sequence guides the interaction dynamics. The resulting rollout has motion close to the source video, but appears under new embodiment or environment. These generated rollouts can be paired with retargeted pseudo robot actions for downstream VLA training. We evaluate RynnWorld-Latent from three complementary perspectives. First, we assess action-conditioned video prediction on public world-model benchmarks and held-out demonstrations from two real-robot platforms, measuring prediction fidelity after target-robot adaptation. Second, we investigate latent-action controllability through qualitative comparisons that vary the supplied latent-action sequences while holding the initial observation fixed, and illustrate cross-embodiment motion transfer through first-frame editing. Third, we examine the utility of world-model-generated data for downstream policy learning. Synthetic mid-training improves success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, while both latent-action-driven synthesis and digital teleoperation improve observed closed-loop policy success on the evaluated real-world manipulation tasks. These evaluations jointly characterize prediction fidelity, qualitative action following, and downstream training utility. Our main contributions are as follows: We present RynnWorld-Latent, text-free, latent-action-conditioned video world model, which uses frozen RynnLAM descriptors as shared conditioning interface for learning visual dynamics from human interaction videos, heterogeneous robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without aligning their native control spaces. We design an action-conditioning mechanism that combines global action tokens with locally identityinitialized, frame-aligned injection, associating transition descriptors with the corresponding future video latents. We enable latent-action-guided generation under edited robot embodiments and environments, and adapt the world model to native robot-action conditioning. The resulting latent-action synthesis and digital-teleoperation pipelines generate data that improves downstream policy learning in the evaluated settings.

sections.title: 2.1 World Models
sections.content: World models predict how environments change under actions and support planning and policy learning through simulated experience (Finn et al., 2016; Ebert et al., 2018; Hafner et al., 2019, 2020). Advances in video generation have enabled large-scale pretraining of visual dynamics models and their adaptation to interactive simulation (Agarwal et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024b; Rigter et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). Language-conditioned video and image generation have also been used to produce visual plans and synthetic demonstrations for robot control (Du et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024b; Jang et al., 2025). However, task-level instructions leave the timing and trajectory of individual movements largely unspecified. To simulate fine-grained manipulation, action-conditioned world models incorporate robot controls into future prediction (Zhu et al., 2025b; Guo et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025b). Such predictions support policy evaluation (Li et al., 2025a; Quevedo et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c) and planning (Ebert et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026), while related approaches combine future prediction with action learning to improve robot policies (Wu et al., 2024a; Cheang et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025a; Ye et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). Extending action-conditioned modeling across embodiments requires handling differences in action dimensions, coordinate conventions, and control semantics. Existing approaches address this through heterogeneous action modeling (Wang et al., 2025b) or geometric motion representations shared by humans and robots (Wu and Gao, 2026; Zhao et al., 2026c). For pretraining on diverse robot and human videos, further challenge is that many data sources lack corresponding control labels. More closely related to our setting, latent-action pretraining infers conditioning variables from observed transitions, allowing videos without native action labels to contribute to world-model learning (Gao et al., 2025; Garrido et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Liu and Shorinwa, 2026). Building on this direction, RynnWorld-Latent uses continuous latent actions as shared conditioning interface for cross-embodiment world-model pretraining, without requiring direct alignment of embodiment-specific control spaces.

sections.title: 2.2 Latent Action Learning
sections.content: Learning across embodiments requires representations that connect different forms of observation and control. Prior work studies shared policies trained on heterogeneous robot data (ONeill et al., 2024; Octo Model Team, 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024) and action-space alignment using recorded controls (Zheng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c). For videos without corresponding robot actions, transferable skills and geometric motion cues provide intermediate representations for learning (Xu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2024; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024; Collins et al., 2025). Latent action learning instead infers compact action variables from transitions between observations (Rybkin et al., 2019; Schmidt and Jiang, 2024). These variables have been used as supervision for policy pretraining and transfer (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Figure 1 Pretraining corpus overview. The corpus contains 23 datasets, approximately 6,190 hours, and 2.57M episodes. The figure summarizes the distribution of human, real-robot, and simulation video, dataset contributions by duration, and object and action vocabulary. Bu et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025b; Tharwat et al., 2025), as well as conditioning inputs for predicting future states (Menapace et al., 2021; Bruce et al., 2024; Alles et al., 2025; Bi et al., 2025; Garrido et al., 2026). Both discrete codes (Bruce et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b) and continuous representations (Gao et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Garrido et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026) have been explored. Recent work further studies alignment with available action supervision (Zhang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026), the separation of motion from appearance (Yang et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b), and geometric constraints on the learned action space (Yang et al., 2026b). These distinctions matter because visual changes can include camera motion, background variation, and other effects unrelated to the agents control (Nikulin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Garrido et al., 2026). Building on these studies, we use pretrained and frozen encoder RynnLAM (Zhao et al., 2026d) to extract 3D-grounded continuous latent-action descriptors from heterogeneous visual transitions. Unlike methods that require native control annotations or explicit motion retargeting during world-model pretraining, our approach uses these descriptors as shared conditioning interface for human, robot, and simulation videos. This enables joint learning of visual dynamics without requiring the original action parameterizations to be aligned across embodiments.

sections.title: 3.5 World-Model Data Engine
sections.content: Figure 2 Overview of the world-model data engine. Top: Scalable data editing. RynnLAM extracts latent actions from source human video, while its first frame is edited to depict the target robot. Conditioned on the edited frame and the original latent actions, RynnWorld-Latent generates robot video rollouts. The generated observations are paired with pseudo-actions obtained through motion retargeting and inverse kinematics. Bottom: Digital teleoperation. Human control signals are retargeted to robot actions, which condition RynnWorld-Latent together with reference scene. Generated frames provide visual feedback to the operator, while the recorded actions and generated observations form synthetic demonstrations without physical robot execution. To generate trajectories for policy learning, we combine the world model with interfaces for capturing interaction intent and producing action-video episodes. In our design, RynnWorld-Latent provides action-conditioned visual dynamics, while the surrounding pipeline provides target-robot adaptation, action retargeting, temporal alignment, and filtering. Compared with asset-based simulation, this generative pipeline can reduce the need for explicit 3D assets and manual system identification: scenes are specified implicitly by conditioning image, visual outputs are produced in learned video distribution, and interaction priors are drawn from large-scale video pretraining. We instantiate two complementary data-generation pipelines: interactive digital teleoperation and latent-action data synthesis. Target-robot adaptation. Before using RynnWorld-Latent for data generation, we post-train it on target robot demonstrations. Our real-robot corpus is shared with RynnVLA-Latent (Zhao et al., 2026d) and contains 3,850 collected episodes across six tasks (Appendix B). For each task, 5% of the episodes are randomly held out for testing and the remaining 95% form the target-robot post-training split; the 3,850-episode count refers to the full collected corpus. The target data is processed with the same chunking protocol and latent-action labeling pipeline. This stage adapts the model to the target embodiments visual appearance, camera configuration, and interaction distribution. Robot-action conditioning is introduced through separate target-specific encoder. When target robot actions are available, we introduce lightweight action encoder Eψ that maps target robot action uj into an action token: τ = Eψ(uj). (7) Figure 3 RynnEdit. Two routes construct robot-centric reference frame: explicit hand removal, retargeting, and robot rendering; or direct replacement of human hands with robotic counterparts using an image-editing model. The resulting first frame conditions subsequent world-model generation. The token τ is injected through the same conditioning pathway as the latent-action token τj. We train this interface with the same rectified-flow video objective, replacing latent-action tokens with robot-action tokens. Here uj denotes the robot-action input synchronized with the interval represented by latent action zj; its parameterization depends on the target robot. The encoder provides an embodiment-specific control interface without requiring commands to share RynnLAMs descriptor dimensions. After this adaptation, RynnWorldLatent can be used not only as latent-action-conditioned world model, but also as an action-conditioned world model for interactive generation. RynnEdit: Robot-centric reference-frame construction pipeline. The data engine requires reference scene frame Iref compatible with the target robots appearance and workspace. However, collecting real-world robot data in new environments is costly. We therefore synthesize scenes featuring the target robot from large-scale egocentric human hand videos. Given an egocentric interaction video, we construct robot-centric initial observation by replacing human hands with the target robot while preserving the background and initial interaction configuration. The resulting first frame conditions the data engine; the source latentaction sequence supplies the subsequent motion. Our pipeline shown in Fig. 3 consists of egocentric data preprocessing followed by two alternative routes for generating robot-centric initial scenes: robot inpainting like Ego2Robot (Wang et al., 2026b) and image editing using an end-to-end model. During preprocessing, we verify the integrity of the input videos and motion data, standardize their formats, and extract egocentric frames and human hand poses. We temporally align the video and motion sequences using zero-order hold or interpolation. We also use SAM3 (Carion et al., 2026), prompted with human hand keypoints and text descriptions, to segment the hands and combine the resulting masks. In the robot inpainting route, we perform video inpainting within the hand masks to reconstruct the background after removing the human hands. We retarget the extracted human hand motion to the robotic hand and estimate the robot base pose and joint configurations through motion post-processing and inverse kinematics with base-pose search in MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012). We then render the robot in the estimated poses and composite the rendered images onto the inpainted background to obtain robotic manipulation observations corresponding to the original human demonstrations. In the image editing route, we instead provide the original egocentric image and its hand mask to an end-to-end image-editing model, like Qwen-Image-Edit (Wu et al., 2025a), which replaces the human hands with robotic counterparts to generate an initial scene. The two routes thus produce synthetic robot observations through explicit retargeting and rendering or direct image editing, respectively. Finally, we apply quality gates to filter the generated observations and retain accepted samples as initial scenes for subsequent world-model-based data generation. Interactive digital teleoperation. The teleoperation pipeline converts operator motion into target robot actions and uses RynnWorld-Latent as the visual rollout engine  (Fig. 2)  . Given an initial conditioning frame Iref and stream of operator control signals, we retarget the operator motion to the target robot action space, producing time-stamped action sequence. In chunk-based generation, the robot commands are synchronized with the video timeline and encoded through Eψ. RynnWorld-Latent conditions on the current frame and the corresponding sequence of robot-action tokens to generate the future video latents. The last generated frame can then be used as the conditioning frame for the next chunk, enabling long-horizon interactive rollouts. Since the system records both the retargeted actions and the generated frames, interactive digital teleoperation directly produces paired action-video episodes without requiring physical robot execution. Latent-action data synthesis. The second pipeline synthesizes new robot data from existing videos using latent-action transfer. Given source video s, we first extract its latent-action sequence As using the frozen to obtain new reference frame I0 that replaces the embodiment LAM. We then edit the first frame 0 or environment while preserving the scene layout, object arrangement, and camera viewpoint as much as possible. The edited frame is encoded as the conditioning latent c, and RynnWorld-Latent generates rollout conditioned on this edited frame and the original latent-action sequence: pθ( c, As) . (8) In this pipeline, first-frame editing specifies the target visual embodiment or environment, while the transferred latent-action sequence guides the generated interaction dynamics. The edited frame implicitly specifies the initial scene configuration without requiring explicit numerical object or robot states. The resulting rollout is encouraged to exhibit motion patterns related to the source interaction under the edited visual conditions. This transfer is approximate, since changes in robot geometry, workspace constraints, contact configurations, or viewpoint may affect whether the source motion remains physically feasible. The world model itself remains text-free: any prompts used by the external image editor only construct the reference frame I0 and do not condition the subsequent video generation. Action relabeling, synchronization, and filtering. For interactive digital teleoperation, target robot actions can be logged directly. For latent-action data synthesis, robot actions can be obtained by relabeling the source motion. When the source video already has robot actions compatible with the target embodiment, those actions can be reused after temporal alignment. Otherwise, we derive pseudo robot actions by estimating the relevant source motion, retargeting it to the target robot workspace, and applying inverse kinematics; implementation details are provided in Appendix C. The pseudo actions are temporally aligned with the generated video in frame-index space. We emphasize that temporal synchronization does not by itself establish physical consistency: the actions come from retargeting or inverse kinematics, while the observations are produced by an independently trained generator. We therefore treat the derived actions as pseudo-labels and filter episodes based on joint limits, motion smoothness, visual quality, temporal consistency, and plausibility of object interactions. The resulting synthetic episodes can be combined with real robot data for downstream VLA training.

4.1 Experimental Setup
World-model implementation. RynnWorld-Latent is built on Cosmos3-Edge (Agarwal et al., 2026), a mixture-
of-transformers video foundation model. We train for 20K optimizer steps with a global batch size of 512,
using AdamW with (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.99), weight decay 0.05, gradient-norm clipping 1.0, a peak learning rate
of 2.26 × 10−4, 500 warmup steps, and linear decay to 10% of the peak. The newly introduced action-facing
modules are re-initialized for the 608-dimensional latent-action space and use a 5× learning-rate multiplier.
Training uses bf16 with FP32 master weights and optimizer states, and a power-function EMA with s = 0.1.
Parallelism uses hybrid-sharded FSDP with shard degree 8 per node and replication degree 4 across nodes.
All videos are trained in 480p aspect-ratio buckets (832 × 480, 640 × 640, 736 × 544, 544 × 736, and 480 × 832).
Policy backbones. For policy experiments, we use π0 (Black et al., 2024a) and π0.5 (Intelligence et al., 2025) as
base VLA models. For all settings, we use the same downstream training protocol unless otherwise specified.
For synthetic pretraining experiments, we use the term mid-training to denote continued pretraining on
synthetic data, and post-training to denote subsequent fine-tuning on target task or robot data.

sections.title: 4.2 Action-Conditioned World-Model Benchmarks
sections.content: We first evaluate RynnWorld-Latent as an action-conditioned world model on both public benchmarks and our own real-robot benchmarks. DreamDojo benchmarks. We consider three evaluation sets introduced by DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026): In-lab Eval, EgoDex Eval, and DreamDojo-HV Eval. These sets probe whether human-video pretraining transfers to object interactions unseen in the robot post-training data. RynnWorld-Latent real-robot benchmarks. To test simulation fidelity on our own hardware, we construct evaluation sets on both robotic platforms by recording ground-truth rollouts across diverse range of bimanual manipulation scenarios and asking the world model to reproduce them from the same initial frame and action sequence. The evaluation episodes cover varied objects, scenes, and contact patterns, spanning both the stationary dexterous setup (Marvin-WUJI) and the mobile gripper setup (Astribot-S1), and use an episode-level split: for each task, we randomly reserve 5% of the recorded episodes for testing and use the remaining 95% for target-robot post-training. Episodes are split before temporal chunking so that chunks from the same demonstration do not appear in both sets. Synthetic corpus. Robot commands are obtained by relabeling the source motion through retargeting and inverse kinematics; implementation details are provided in Appendix C. Fig. 6 illustrates this pipeline. Large-scale synthesis corpus. We apply this pipeline to EPIC-KITCHENS (Damen et al., 2020), EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2025), and Something-Something (Goyal et al., 2017). The latent interface additionally allows videos without native robot controls to contribute to pretraining; the present ablation does not separately identify how much of the observed gain comes from representation design versus access to additional video data. Conditioning architecture. Removing frame-aligned injection while retaining global action tokens decreases PSNR by 0.72 on Marvin-WUJI and 0.88 on Astribot-S1. These results support combining global action tokens with local frame-aligned conditioning, while indicating that the additive pathway retains useful conditioning when modulation is removed. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented RynnWorld-Latent, cross-embodiment video world model that uses shared continuous latent actions as conditioning interface for learning visual dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos. Building on the 3D-grounded RynnLAM representation, the model combines global action tokens with temporally aligned local conditioning to connect motion descriptors with future video latents. This enables world-model pretraining across human, robot, and simulation videos without requiring their native action spaces to be aligned, followed by target-robot adaptation through an embodiment-specific action encoder. Experiments show strong video prediction fidelity on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, while qualitative comparisons demonstrate that generated motions respond to different supplied latent-action sequences under the same initial observation. The model also supports approximate cross-embodiment motion transfer and native-action-conditioned digital teleoperation. Synthetic data generated through both routes improves downstream policy success in the evaluated settings. Together, these findings support shared latent actions as practical interface for cross-embodiment world-model learning and controllable robot-data generation. Limitations. Latent actions are inferred from observed visual transitions and may encode camera motion or appearance information as well as manipulation. Qualitative action following and image-based prediction metrics therefore do not establish causal identification or physical correctness. In the synthesis pipeline, retargeted robot commands and generated observations are obtained through separate processes; temporal alignment and filtering cannot guarantee their physical consistency. The reported real-world success rates use 35 trials per task, and small differences should be interpreted accordingly. Moreover, synthetic mid-training adds both data and optimization compute, whose contributions are not separated by the current comparisons. Future work will address long-horizon consistency, action-observation alignment, and broader transfer across embodiments.

sections.title: A Teleoperation Setup
sections.content: For Marvin-WUJI, we collect real-world demonstrations through the teleoperation system shown in Fig. 8. The hardware setup consists of dual Tianji 7-DOF robotic arms and dual Wuji 20-DOF dexterous hands, yielding total of 54 degrees of freedom. For arm control, the human operator wears five HTC Vive trackers (mounted on the chest, both wrists, and both upper arms). The system computes wrist-to-chest relative transforms at 100-120 Hz and feeds them into Pinocchio-based inverse kinematics solver running in separate process. The resulting joint commands are further smoothed by Ruckig trajectory generator with velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints before being sent to the robot arms at 200 Hz. For hand control, the operator wears Manus data gloves. The raw glove signals are converted to 21-point MediaPipe hand skeleton format and retargeted to the 20-DOF Wuji hand joint space via dedicated retargeting module, with an exponential moving average filter applied for motion smoothing. Real-World Demonstration Corpus The physically collected demonstration corpus is the same as that used in RynnVLA-Latent (?). It contains 3,850 episodes across six manipulation tasks on the real-robot platforms described in Sec. 4. Tab. 7 reports the collected episode counts. These counts describe the full corpus, not the number of episodes in an individual post-training split or the amount of generated digital-teleoperation data. For world-model adaptation and evaluation, we randomly split episodes within each task into 95% for post-training and 5% for testing. The split is defined at the episode level before video chunking. Thus all chunks from held-out episode remain outside the post-training split, and the test tasks themselves are represented in training. The downstream policy experiments in this paper evaluate four of the six collected tasks. sections.title: C Details of Pseudo Robot Action Relabeling
sections.content: For source videos without target robot actions, we estimate the relevant hand or end-effector trajectory from the source motion. The estimated trajectory is retargeted to the target robot workspace through coordinate mapping, workspace scaling, and embodiment-specific retargeting. We then solve inverse kinematics to obtain target robot joint commands. During IK solving, we enforce joint limits, velocity limits, and temporal smoothness. The resulting actions are treated as pseudo-labels rather than ground-truth robot commands. These pseudo-labels are subsequently filtered together with the generated videos before being used for policy training.

sections.title: D Baseline Implementation Details
sections.content: Ego2Robot. We reproduce Ego2Robot (Wang et al., 2026b) in our pipeline. Specifically, we audit each raw video and its corresponding HaWoR (Zhang et al., 2025b) motion-capture trajectory, geometrically retarget the HaWoR hand poses to the 20-degree-of-freedom (DoF) Wuji hand, and resample the trajectories using zero-order hold or interpolation. At the source resolution, we use the projected HaWoR keypoints as prompts for SAM3 (Carion et al., 2026) to segment both hands and refine the segmentation using text prompts. We then take the union of the leftand right-hand masks, dilate it by 4 pixels, and remove the hands using video object removal model, such as MiniMax-Remover (Zi et al., 2026) or ProPainter (Zhou et al., 2023). In parallel, on the CPU, we estimate the robot base pose through coarse-to-fine inverse kinematics (IK) search in MuJoCo, evaluating 81 candidates in the coarse stage. The visual strategy is decoupled from the segmentation masks, and this branch outputs qpos54 and an IK report. Finally, we render the TIANJI M6 arm and Wuji hand using MuJoCos EGL-based off-screen rasterization and composite the rendered robot onto the inpainted video using an end-effector-locked projection strategy. We further introduce quality gates for sample selection. sample is marked as suitable for training only if it passes both the inpainting content quality checks and the strict IK and projection thresholds. The inpainting checks require peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) outside the removal mask of at least 30 dB, relaxed to 22 dB for videos with camera motion; the absence of entirely black frames; and successful checks of per-frame spatial standard deviation and temporal response. The rendering criteria require position error of at most 5 mm, rotation error of at most 5, an end-effector projection error of at most 3 pixels, 95th-percentile retargeting landmark error of at most 0.1, and finger-direction consistency score of at least 0.9.
